newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thais to feel pain before gain from currency float.
newsitem.headline: Thais to feel pain before gain from currency float.

text.p: Thailand will feel pain before any gains from the floating of the baht, economists and analysts said on Thursday.
The trade deficit was likely to widen due to soaring import bills and inflation would rise, they said.
And gross domestic product growth would likely fall well below five percent with corporates hard hit by swelling foreign debt.

On the plus side, authorities were keeping their fingers crossed the defacto devaluation would attract much-needed foreign inflows to avert a balance of payments crisis. The current account deficit was likely to widen first but narrow later if the trade and services accounts improved.
The more flexible baht would also give the central bank breathing room to manage its interest rate policy more effectively.

"At a more fundamental level, it is well known that a fixed exchange rate, capital mobility and effective monetary policy cannot coexist," said Supavudh Saicheau, vice president of Phatra Thanakit Plc.
Thailand on Thursday opened a new chapter in its financial policy by scrapping the tightly controlled exchange rate regime and allowing the overvalued baht to fall under a new managed-float system.

The basket system, under which the baht was pegged against various currencies in the trade-weighted basket, had benefited Thailand for more than a decade but became a liability when Thailand's economy and external balance started to deteriorate.
The central bank had almost no control over interest rates. It had to keep rates high, even when the economy faced its worst downturn in over a decade, to defend the currency.
Analysts said the overvalued baht and uncertainties over its fate eroded the competitiveness of Thai exports and hampered foreign inflows.
The financial crisis had led to a serious problem with the balance of payments which recorded a 112.3 billion baht deficit in May, jumping from 15.5 billion baht in April.
These twin crises left the government with little option but to adjust its currency system.
After the change, the baht sank to around 28.900 to the dollar from around 25.10 before the float.
Charl Kengchon, economist at Thai Farmers Bank, said the benefit of the devalued baht on exports was overrated as a big percentage of exports depended on imported raw materials and capital goods.
"The change will widen the trade deficit as the imports bill will rise immediately. The benefit on the exports will be very limited near-term," he said.
Charl said the weakening baht would increase the cost of production due to more expensive oil and raw materials. Around 40 percent of Thai exports depend on imported materials.
Economists said agricultural commodities such as rice, rubber, tapioca and sugar would benefit from the move but such exports accounted for only 10-15 percent of all exports revenue.
Corporates with high unhedged foreign loans will be hit by the baht float.

It has been privately estimated that at the end of May, Thailand had $85 billion of foreign debt. Of this, $66 billion was owed by the private sector, and mostly borrowed through facilities with maturities of a year or less.
On the positive side, the float could induce more foreign inflows needed to boost liquidity, analysts said.
Foreigners have swamped the stock market to buy cheap stocks since the float was announced on Wednesday. Prices were up more than eight percent in late Thursday trade.
But is the worst over? May be not, said ING Baring's Varut.
"Generally, a lot of people seem optimistic about the move. But threats remain," he said.
"If the government failed in its effort to restructure the finance sector, we could see the reverse of these inflows again."
